vignette:
Ajay sits stiffly in the chair, a man of seventy-nine whose posture still carries a trace of military bearing. His hands, resting on his knees, are gnarled and calloused from a lifetime of manual labor. For the last forty years, he has worked in warehouses, and he still puts in three shifts a week at a large distribution center on the outskirts of the city. He came to the clinic at the firm insistence of his daughter, who made the appointment for him. He speaks in a low, measured voice, offering only the most basic facts of his life, his gaze fixed on a point just past the therapist's shoulder. He is divorced and lives alone in a small apartment. He has worked hard, he says, and provided for his family. That is what a man does.

He is reluctant to speak of his time as a young soldier in the Indian Army, dismissing it as a lifetime ago, another world. With gentle prompting, he confirms the year was 1971, during the conflict that led to the creation of Bangladesh. He was part of a patrol sent into the dense, swampy jungles near the border. The air was thick with moisture and the drone of insects. He remembers the sudden, deafening crack of rifle fire from the tree line. The world dissolved into shouts, muzzle flashes, and the metallic smell of cordite. He saw his friend, a boy from a neighboring village he had known his whole life, fall beside him without a sound. The engagement was brief but savage, a chaotic whirlwind of violence that ended as quickly as it began. He was one of only three men from his patrol to walk out of that jungle clearing. He does not elaborate on what followed.

After his service, Ajay sought a different life. He emigrated to the United States in the late 1970s, settling in a small South Asian community. He met and married a woman, and they had two children, a son and a daughter. He found steady work, first loading trucks and eventually becoming a certified forklift operator, a job he found satisfying in its simplicity and order. He speaks of his divorce twenty years ago in a single, unadorned sentence, offering no context or emotion. It is presented as just another fact, like his place of birth or his current address. He continued to work, to send money to his children for their education, and to keep to himself.

His life remains one of routine. He wakes before dawn for the early shift, the cavernous warehouse a familiar landscape of towering metal shelves and the steady hum of machinery. He is known as a quiet, dependable worker who never misses a day. Recently, however, his supervisor took him aside to express concern. He had seemed distracted, less focused on the task at hand. His daughter, during her weekly visits, noticed a change as well, a deeper silence that had settled over him. It was she who finally told him he needed to talk to someone, that he couldn't carry whatever it was he was carrying alone anymore.

When asked what brings him here today, Ajay is quiet for a long time. He looks down at his weathered hands, turning them over as if seeing them for the first time. "My daughter is worried," he says finally. "I do not want to be a burden to her." He offers little else about his own state of mind. Initial screening with the PCL-5 reveals a score of 65, indicating a profound level of post-traumatic distress that stands in stark contrast to his stoic and guarded presentation. He has carried the weight of that day in the jungle for over fifty years, and the precise nature of that burden-the shape of the memories, the content of his fears, the landscape of his inner world-remains, for now, entirely his own.
